hints: Focus on what heating these gases could do, and what coloured vapours would tell you about decomposition.
Recall the colours: bromine vapour is brown and iodine vapour is purple, so match each vapour to its parent hydrogen halide.
Compare bond strengths: the H-I bond is weaker than the H-Br bond, so think about which gas will break apart first on heating.
walkthrough:
**Spot what the colours mean**

Think of heating as a test of thermal stability. If the gas breaks down, you see the halogen.

$$2\text{HBr(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \text{Br}_2\text{(g, brown)}$$ 
$$2\text{HI(g)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{(g)} + \text{I}_2\text{(g, purple)}$$

**Compare H-Br and H-I bond strength**

Bond strength decreases down Group 17 because the atoms get larger and overlap gets poorer. That makes H-I weaker and easier to break than H-Br.

Bond strength order: $\text{H-Cl} > \text{H-Br} > \text{H-I}$

**Decide which decomposes first**

Because HI is less thermally stable, it will decompose to purple $\text{I}_2$ vapour at a temperature where HBr is still unchanged. It is impossible for HBr to decompose while HI stays unchanged at the same temperature.

options.A: Incorrect. Brown vapour means Br2 from HBr decomposing, while HI shows no change. This is backwards because HI has the weaker bond and must decompose before HBr does.
options.B: Incorrect. Purple vapour is I2, which cannot come from HBr. Also, it claims HBr changes while HI does not, which contradicts the stability trend H-Br stronger than H-I.
options.C: Incorrect. It correctly has HBr unchanged, but brown vapour cannot come from HI. Decomposition of HI gives purple iodine vapour, not brown bromine vapour.
options.D: Correct. HI is thermally less stable than HBr, so on heating HI decomposes to H2 and purple I2 vapour while HBr remains unchanged at the same temperature.
